ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Rheumatology Referral — Flannery O'Connor

code.originalText: Primary care visit for joint pain and swelling, fevers, fatigue, a facial rash, and protein in the urine in a writer of 25

text.paragraph: Inflammatory polyarthritis with fevers, fatigue, a malar-pattern rash, leukopenia, lymphopenia, mild anemia and thrombocytopenia, and protein and blood in the urine in a woman of 25. I suspect systemic lupus erythematosus with kidney involvement rather than rheumatoid arthritis. Please confirm the diagnosis, assess the kidneys, and plan treatment with her. [S]
Urgency: Urgent, within ten days, because of the urine findings. [S]

list.item: Does she have systemic lupus erythematosus, and which tests confirm it and define organ involvement?
Do the urine findings mean lupus nephritis, and does she need a kidney biopsy?
What treatment do you recommend, including hydroxychloroquine, how to keep glucocorticoids low, and which immunosuppressive or biologic drugs?
Which vaccinations and infection screening should come before immunosuppression?
What contraception is suitable, and how should a future pregnancy be planned?
How should bone health, avascular necrosis, and the eyes be protected and monitored?
She knows that her father had lupus: how should that family history shape her counseling?

text.paragraph: Three months of pain and swelling in the small joints of both hands, the wrists, and the knees, with an hour of morning stiffness, evening fevers to 38 °C, fatigue, and a red rash over the cheeks and nose after sun; she was told elsewhere it might be rheumatoid arthritis. Today: temperature 37.9 °C, blood pressure 138/86. White cells 3.3, lymphocytes 0.8, hemoglobin 11.0, platelets 138; creatinine 0.8, eGFR 101, albumin 3.3; ESR 52, CRP 0.6; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.6 g/g with 18 red cells per high-power field. PHQ-9 7. An operation for a floating kidney some years ago. Her father had lupus. No medicines except acetaminophen as needed; no NSAIDs advised. No known allergy. Sexually active without contraception; would like children some day. She is a writer finishing her first novel. She asks for plain, complete answers, given to her directly, and that her diagnosis not be shared with anyone she has not named [S]

list.item: Painful, swollen hands and knees, fevers, tiredness, and a rash on her face, for three months. [S]
Wants a plain, complete answer about what is wrong, told to her directly, and asks that it not be shared with anyone she has not named. [S]
Afraid of losing her writing mornings to illness or treatment. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Flannery O'Connor was born in Savannah, Georgia, on March 25, 1925, the only child of Edward Francis O'Connor and Regina Cline O'Connor. She later dropped her first name for her writing. [D]

Her father was diagnosed with lupus in 1937; his illness began with a whitish patch of skin on his forehead and arthritis, and was first diagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. He died of systemic lupus erythematosus in 1941, a month after his 45th birthday, when she was 15. [D]

O'Connor graduated from Georgia State College for Women in 1945 and then studied at the Writers' Workshop of the State University of Iowa, where she earned a Master of Fine Arts; she was writing her first novel by the late 1940s. [D]
In December 1949, at 24, she fell seriously ill on a holiday visit to Georgia and spent about a month in hospital, where she had an operation for a floating kidney. [D]

Inflammatory arthritis with fever, rash, cytopenias, and an abnormal urine: blood count, chemistry, ESR and CRP, urine microscopy and protein-to-creatinine ratio today; ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, complements, and antiphospholipid antibodies; no NSAIDs with protein in the urine. Sun protection: broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 50 or higher, a wide-brimmed hat, and shade in the middle of the day. Guideline: EULAR recommendations for the management of systemic lupus erythematosus: 2023 update. Ann Rheum Dis 2024;83(1):15-29 (2023) [S]
